tweets.text:
I get this question a lot:

“Would you ever consider shorting a stock that looks technically weak?”

My answer is always no.

We’re trading in such a juiced environment during an AI and technology revolution that it only takes one headline, contract announcement, partnership, or catalyst to completely change the technical picture overnight.

Not to mention, how many times have we watched a stock look absolutely awful technically, only for it to violently reverse the next day or week and rip right back up?

There are plenty of ways to make money in this market without taking on that kind of asymmetric headline risk.

For me, shorting is a zero-sum game in this environment. I’d rather stay patient, keep cash on the sidelines, and wait for high-quality long setups.

tweets.text:
Another underrated benefit of getting a great cost basis in a high-conviction stock and simply not trading around it: taxes.

You sell a winner, realize the gains, and rotate into something else. Then the new position rolls over or simply doesn’t do what you anticipated.

Now you’re on the hook for taxes from the realized gains while simultaneously sitting on an unrealized loss in the new position.

Suddenly you feel compelled to cut that position before year-end just to offset some of the previous gains.

And, of course, the second you sell both names, they’ll probably rip without you.

Sometimes the best trade really is doing nothing.
